findings.claim: Eduqas examiners flag this confusion every year.
findings.truth: House rule: an Eduqas/WJEC lesson never names the board in student prose, and no examiner statement is quoted or citable. The point itself is sound, so it is restated without the board and without the examiner claim.
findings.evidence: house rule; no citable examiner source

findings.claim: Eduqas examiners flag two predictable mistakes on this topic.
findings.truth: Same house rule: board named plus an invented examiner claim. Reworded to 'Two mistakes come up again and again'.

findings.claim: More than nine million UK workers commute across the urban-rural boundary every weekday.
findings.truth: No published statistic supports nine million. The whole rural population of the UK is about 17 per cent of roughly 67 million people, so nine million cross-boundary commuters is not credible. Reduced to 'Millions of UK workers', which is true on every published figure.
findings.evidence: ONS rural-urban population share; no source for the nine million claim

findings.claim: Net migration peaked at around 745,000 in 2022 before falling to roughly 600,000 in the year to mid-2023. Repeated in the key fact and in a flashcard answer (600,000).
findings.truth: The ONS revised series puts the peak at 944,000 in the year ending March 2023, then a sharp fall to 649,000 (YE June 2024) and 204,000 (YE June 2025). Both the peak value and the direction of travel in the lesson are wrong: net migration rose into 2023, it did not fall. Corrected to 944,000 (YE March 2023) falling to about 204,000 (YE June 2025).
findings.evidence: ONS Long-term international migration, year ending June 2025 bulletin

findings.claim: The Office for National Statistics calls this the 'greying' of Britain.
findings.truth: The ONS does not use this phrase for the ageing population. The phrase is journalistic. The attribution is removed; the phrase itself stays.
findings.evidence: no ONS source for the phrase

findings.claim: Following relaxed permitted-development rules in 2020, an estimated 70,000 office-to-residential conversions were created in England by 2023.
findings.truth: The permitted development right that lets offices become homes without full planning permission was introduced in May 2013 (made permanent in 2016); 2020-21 brought a separate commercial-to-residential right. The date is wrong and the 70,000 figure is not tied to a published series, so the number is dropped and the date corrected to 2013.
findings.evidence: Town and Country Planning (General Permitted Development) Order office-to-residential right, 2013

findings.claim: 1.6 children per woman is called the 'birth rate' in the key fact, the conclusion, knowledge check 1, flashcard 1 and practice question 1 - while the lesson's own glossary defines birth rate as 'the number of live births per 1,000 people'.
findings.truth: 1.6 children per woman is the total fertility rate, not the birth rate. The lesson contradicts its own definition. Every place where 1.6 is labelled 'birth rate' is relabelled 'fertility rate'; the glossary definition and the numbers are unchanged.
findings.evidence: ONS births in England and Wales (TFR 1.61 in 2021); lesson glossary

findings.claim: Eduqas examiners often ask candidates to use specific places.
findings.truth: Board named in student prose plus an invented examiner claim. Reworded to 'The exam often asks you to use specific places.'

findings.claim: The GBP 40 million Globe theatre reopened in 2021.
findings.truth: The Stockton Globe restoration started with a GBP 4 million budget and finished at GBP 27.9 million. The reopening year (2021) is right.

findings.claim: a 3,000-seat live-music venue - repeated in the key fact, knowledge check 3, flashcard 8 and practice question 5.
findings.truth: The Globe seats about 2,372. 3,000 is the full capacity with standing, so 'seat' is wrong and 'capacity' is right. Changed in all five places so the answer keys stay consistent.

findings.claim: Internet shopping rose ... to a peak of 38% during the 2020 lockdown.
findings.truth: The ONS internet-sales ratio reached its record high of about 37.8 per cent in early 2021, during the third lockdown, not in 2020. Changed to 'during the pandemic lockdowns', which is true of the whole 2020-21 peak.
findings.evidence: ONS retail sales internet sales ratio series

findings.claim: For Eduqas you must study one city in a high-income country (HIC) and one in a low- or newly-industrialised country (LIC/NIC).
findings.truth: The requirement itself is correct (spec 2.3.2 requires one HIC city and one LIC/NIC city, and India is on the spec's NIC list), but the board must not be named in student prose. Changed to 'For this course'.
findings.evidence: spec 2.3.2 and Appendix B; house rule

findings.claim: Eduqas examiner reports stress that 'a city in Africa' or 'a city in Asia' loses marks at 6 and 8 mark tariffs.
findings.truth: Board named plus a cited-but-unquoted examiner report. The advice is sound and is kept without the attribution.

findings.claim: the 2021 census found over 300 languages spoken
findings.truth: The '300-plus languages' figure comes from research into the home languages of London schoolchildren (Baker and Eversley, 2000), not from the 2021 census, which recorded main language in a much shorter list. The figure is kept, the false attribution removed.
findings.evidence: census 2021 language outputs do not contain this figure

findings.claim: the city is India's busiest port - repeated in the conclusion and in the practice question 2 answer key.
findings.truth: Mumbai's own docks are not India's busiest port. Mundra (Gujarat) is India's biggest container port and Jawaharlal Nehru Port in Navi Mumbai is the next biggest and the Mumbai region's main port. Corrected to name Jawaharlal Nehru Port as one of India's biggest container ports, which keeps the connectivity point the spec asks for (2.3.3).

findings.claim: Cardiff Bay 'has 6,000 new homes, 25,000 jobs and tourism brings around 5 million visitors a year' - the three figures also drive the key fact, two practice answer keys and two flashcards.
findings.truth: Everything else in the Cardiff Bay case study checks out (CBDC 1987, barrage completed 1999, 1.1 km long, 200-hectare freshwater lake, Wales Millennium Centre 2004, Senedd 2006). The three output figures could not be verified from Wikipedia or an official page in this session, and published summaries of the CBDC's outputs vary widely on jobs. Options: (a) leave the figures as they are; (b) check them against Cardiff Council or Welsh Government regeneration figures and correct all six places together. Recommendation: leave them for now and add them to a targeted source check - a partial correction across six fields is worse than none.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Cardiff Bay (confirms barrage, lake and CBDC dates only)
findings.ruling: Leave: unverified / not worth the ripple.

findings.claim: over 50 million passengers passed through Chhatrapati Shivaji International Airport in 2019 - repeated in the practice question 2 answer key and in the knowledge check 5 matching option ('International airport with over 50 million passengers a year' matched to 'Both').
findings.truth: Mumbai's airport handled about 49.8 million passengers in 2018 and did not clear 50 million before the pandemic, so 'over 50 million' is just false. Heathrow (79 million) clears it easily, so the 'Both' match is the weak link. Options: (a) leave it - the overstatement is under half a per cent and no student loses a mark on it; (b) change three fields to 'nearly 50 million' and reword the matching option. Recommendation: leave it; the edit cost outweighs a 0.2 million overstatement.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj International Airport (49.8 million in 2018)
findings.ruling: Leave: unverified / not worth the ripple.

findings.claim: A 2023 Rural England report found that around 17 % of rural households experience fuel poverty ... Remote rural wages are about 10 % below the urban average ... bus services have been cut by over 50 % in some counties since 2010.
findings.truth: Rural England is a real body that publishes State of Rural Services reports, and all three figures are in the plausible range, but none could be checked against a source in this session. Not edited.

findings.claim: From the 1860s the Bay was a working dock exporting Welsh coal.
findings.truth: Cardiff's first dock, the Bute West Dock, opened in 1839; coal exports peaked in 1913. The 1860s date understates the start by about 25 years but does not change the geography being taught.

findings.claim: When complete around 2030, Northstowe will have 10,000 homes ... Power comes partly from a community-scale solar farm.
findings.truth: The 10,000 homes, 24,000 residents, former RAF airfield site, guided-bus link and 30 per cent affordable share all match published Northstowe material. The completion date looks optimistic (build-out now runs well past 2030) and the solar farm claim was not verified. Not edited.

findings.claim: the Metro Centre supports about 9,000 jobs ... By 2024 fewer than 35% of retail sales happened there [the high street] ... By 2020 there were more than 1,500 retail parks in the UK.
findings.truth: Metrocentre employment is usually reported as over 7,000, and neither the 35 per cent high-street share nor the 1,500 retail parks could be tied to a source. The Metrocentre opening year (1986), floor space (2 million sq ft) and parking (10,000 spaces) all check out. Not edited.

findings.claim: Department stores have collapsed: BHS in 2016, House of Fraser stores throughout the 2010s, Wilko in 2023.
findings.truth: Wilko was a variety and hardware chain, not a department store. The dates are right (BHS 2016, House of Fraser administration 2018, Wilko 2023). Not edited.

findings.claim: Bollywood (the world's largest film industry by volume)
findings.truth: Indian cinema as a whole makes more films than any other country's, but Bollywood is only its Hindi-language part and in recent years has not even been the largest Indian industry by output. Not edited.

findings.claim: Garden villages such as Northstowe near Cambridge and Bicester in Oxfordshire are large planned greenfield expansions.
findings.truth: Bicester is a designated garden town and Northstowe a new town built partly on a former RAF site; neither is a garden village, and Northstowe's core is brownfield (as lesson 3 itself says). Not edited.

summary: Scope and exam framing are right: all five lessons sit inside Core Theme 2 (urban-rural continuum, population and urban change, Egan's wheel with a brownfield and a greenfield context, retail change, two contrasting global cities with India on the spec's NIC list), the 8 marks plus 4 SPaG label matches this paper's 84 marks plus 4 SPaG, and all 25 knowledge-check keys and 5 matching sets are correct. The damage is in three places: six exam tips and key facts name the board or invent examiner claims; the UK net migration figures in lesson 2 are wrong in both value and direction against the revised ONS series; and case-study numbers in lesson 4 (Globe theatre cost and seating) and lesson 5 (Mumbai's port, the 300-languages attribution) do not survive checking. Lesson 3 needs no edit.
